items.stem: Define accommodation.
items.answer: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to see near and far objects clearly
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Accommodation – the ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to see near and far objects clearly.

items.stem: Which part of the eye changes the focal length of the eye lens?
items.answer: the ciliary muscles
items.markingKey: (b) The ciliary muscles — changes the focal length of the eye lens. The others: the retina – converts light into electrical signals; the optic nerve – carries signals to the brain; the pupil – controls the amount of light entering the eye.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The pupil becomes smaller in bright light.
Reason (R): The iris controls the size of the pupil.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Assume the eye lens is 2.5 cm from the retina. What focal length must the eye lens have to see (a) a distant object (b) an object 50 cm away clearly? What does this show?
items.answer: (a) 2.5 cm (b) 2.38 cm; the eye lens must become more convex (shorter focal length) for near objects — accommodation.

items.stem: Assume the eye lens is 2.5 cm from the retina. What focal length must the eye lens have to see (a) a distant object (b) an object 40 cm away clearly? What does this show?
items.answer: (a) 2.5 cm (b) 2.35 cm; the eye lens must become more convex (shorter focal length) for near objects — accommodation.

items.stem: Assume the eye lens is 2.5 cm from the retina. What focal length must the eye lens have to see (a) a distant object (b) an object 30 cm away clearly? What does this show?
items.answer: (a) 2.5 cm (b) 2.31 cm; the eye lens must become more convex (shorter focal length) for near objects — accommodation.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye on which the image is formed."
items.answer: the retina
items.markingKey: (b) The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye on which the image is formed.

items.stem: Why is a normal eye unable to see clearly objects placed closer than 25 cm?
items.answer: The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum, so the image of a very close object cannot be focused on the retina.
items.markingKey: 2 marks.

items.stem: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering the eye?
items.answer: the pupil
items.markingKey: (c) The pupil — controls the amount of light entering the eye. The others: the ciliary muscles – changes the focal length of the eye lens; the optic nerve – carries signals to the brain; the retina – converts light into electrical signals.

items.stem: Which part of the eye converts light into electrical signals?
items.answer: the retina
items.markingKey: (a) The retina — converts light into electrical signals. The others: the ciliary muscles – changes the focal length of the eye lens; the pupil – controls the amount of light entering the eye; the iris – controls the amount of light entering the eye.

items.stem: Assume the eye lens is 2.5 cm from the retina. What focal length must the eye lens have to see (a) a distant object (b) an object 25 cm away clearly? What does this show?
items.answer: (a) 2.5 cm (b) 2.27 cm; the eye lens must become more convex (shorter focal length) for near objects — accommodation.

items.stem: A myopic person uses spectacles with:
items.answer: concave lenses
items.markingKey: (d) concave lenses.

items.stem: Which of these is a feature of presbyopia?
items.answer: often corrected with bifocal lenses
items.markingKey: (a) Often corrected with bifocal lenses is a feature of presbyopia. The others: image of distant objects formed in front of the retina – a feature of myopia; image of nearby objects formed behind the retina – a feature of hypermetropia; eyeball too short – a feature of hypermetropia.
options: image of distant objects formed in front of the retina
image of nearby objects formed behind the retina

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Hypermetropia is corrected with a concave lens.
Reason (R): In hypermetropia the near point is farther than 25 cm.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Sort these into a feature of myopia and a feature of presbyopia: (1) weakening of the ciliary muscles with age; (2) corrected with a concave lens; (3) decreasing flexibility of the eye lens with age; (4) elongation of the eyeball.
items.answer: A feature of myopia: corrected with a concave lens; elongation of the eyeball. A feature of presbyopia: decreasing flexibility of the eye lens with age; weakening of the ciliary muscles with age.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A feature of myopia: corrected with a concave lens; elongation of the eyeball. A feature of presbyopia: decreasing flexibility of the eye lens with age; weakening of the ciliary muscles with age.

items.stem: Nandini cannot see objects beyond 1.5 m clearly. Name the defect and find the nature, focal length and power of the lens needed.
items.answer: Myopia; concave lens of focal length −150 cm and power −0.67 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form an image of a distant object at the far point: u = ∞, v = −150 cm ⇒ f = −150 cm = −1.5 m; P = 1/f = −0.67 D.

items.stem:
Read: Meera, a Class X student, finds it hard to read the blackboard from the last bench but can read the textbook easily. An optometrist finds that the student's far point is 125 cm.
(i) Name the defect. (ii) Give one possible cause. (iii) What is the type and power of the lens needed? (iv) Draw (describe) how the lens corrects the defect.
items.answer: (i) Myopia. (ii) Excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. (iii) Concave lens of power −0.8 D (f = −125 cm). (iv) The concave lens diverges parallel rays so they appear to come from the far point, and the eye focuses them on the retina.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: A person has a far point of 125 cm and a near point of 100 cm. (a) Name the two defects. (b) Find the power of the lens needed to correct distant vision. (c) Find the power needed for reading at 25 cm. (d) What type of spectacles would suit this person? (e) Give one cause of each defect.
items.answer: (a) Myopia and hypermetropia (presbyopia). (b) −0.8 D (concave). (c) +3 D (convex). (d) Bifocal lenses – concave upper part, convex lower part. (e) Myopia: elongated eyeball/excess curvature; hypermetropia: short eyeball/long focal length (weak ciliary muscles with age).

items.stem: The far point of a myopic eye is 50 cm. The power of the corrective lens is:
A student sitting at the back of the class cannot read the blackboard but can read her book. What defect does she have, what type of lens should she use, and why?
items.answer: Myopia: the image of distant objects forms in front of the retina; a concave lens of suitable power diverges the rays so the image forms on the retina.
items.markingKey: 1 mark defect. 1 mark lens. 1 mark reason.

items.stem: The near point of Aditi's grandfather is 75 cm. What power of lens is needed for him to read a book at 25 cm? Name the defect and the type of lens.
items.answer: Hypermetropia; convex lens of focal length 37.5 cm, power +2.67 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form a virtual image of the book (u = −25 cm) at the near point (v = −75 cm). 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/75 + 1/25 ⇒ f = 37.5 cm; P = 100/f = +2.67 D.

items.stem: The near point of Fatima's grandfather is 125 cm. What power of lens is needed for him to read a book at 25 cm? Name the defect and the type of lens.
items.answer: Hypermetropia; convex lens of focal length 31.2 cm, power +3.2 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form a virtual image of the book (u = −25 cm) at the near point (v = −125 cm). 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/125 + 1/25 ⇒ f = 31.2 cm; P = 100/f = +3.2 D.

items.stem: The near point of Kabir's grandfather is 50 cm. What power of lens is needed for him to read a book at 25 cm? Name the defect and the type of lens.
items.answer: Hypermetropia; convex lens of focal length 50 cm, power +2 D

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The minimum distance (about 25 cm for a normal eye) at which objects can be seen clearly without strain."
items.answer: the near point
items.markingKey: (b) The near point is the minimum distance (about 25 cm for a normal eye) at which objects can be seen clearly without strain.

items.stem: Why is eye donation encouraged?
items.answer: Corneal blindness can be cured by transplanting corneas from donated eyes; one pair of eyes can give vision to up to four people.
items.markingKey: 2 marks.

items.stem: What is meant by the angle of the prism?
items.answer: The angle between two lateral faces of a prism
items.markingKey: 1 mark: The angle of the prism – the angle between two lateral faces of a prism.

items.stem: Which of the two colours, green or violet, is deviated less by a glass prism?
items.answer: green
items.markingKey: (a) Deviation increases from red to violet (VIBGYOR order: violet most, red least).

items.stem: Why can a rainbow be seen only when the Sun is behind the observer?
items.answer: Raindrops act like tiny prisms that refract, disperse and internally reflect sunlight back towards the side of the Sun, so the observer must face away from it.
items.markingKey: 2 marks.

items.stem: Arrange these colours in decreasing order of the deviation they suffer in a prism: green, violet, red, indigo.
items.answer: violet > indigo > green > red
items.markingKey: Violet is deviated most and red least: V > I > B > G > Y > O > R.

items.answer: blue > green > yellow > red
items.markingKey: Violet is deviated most and red least: V > I > B > G > Y > O > R.

items.stem: Two beams of red and violet light enter a prism. Which emerges with the larger deviation, and what does this tell you about their speeds in glass?
items.answer: Violet is deviated more; it travels more slowly in glass (higher refractive index) than red.
items.markingKey: 1 mark violet. 1 mark slower. 1 mark refractive index.

items.stem:
Read: Rohit, standing on a roof in Shillong after a shower, saw a rainbow in the east in the evening. He also noticed that the setting Sun looked red and that the sky overhead was blue.
(i) Why was the rainbow in the east? (ii) Name the three processes in raindrops that form a rainbow. (iii) Why did the setting Sun look red? (iv) Why is the sky overhead blue?
items.answer: (i) The Sun was in the west; a rainbow forms opposite to the Sun. (ii) Refraction, dispersion and internal reflection. (iii) Light travels a long path through air at sunset, blue light is scattered away and red reaches the eye. (iv) Air molecules scatter blue light more.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Why does the sky appear blue to us but black on the Moon? What colour would the sky appear if the Earth had no atmosphere?
items.answer: Air molecules scatter blue light; the Moon has no atmosphere, so no scattering and the sky is dark; without an atmosphere the Earth's sky would also appear dark.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The spreading of light in different directions by particles in its path."

items.answer: Water droplets in clouds are large and scatter all colours almost equally, so the scattered light looks white.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a result of atmospheric refraction?
items.answer: the black sky seen by astronauts
items.markingKey: (b) The black sky seen by astronauts is a result of scattering of light, not a result of atmospheric refraction. Each of the others (the flattened appearance of the Sun at sunrise, advanced sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes, twinkling of stars) is a result of atmospheric refraction.
options: the black sky seen by astronauts
the flattened appearance of the Sun at sunrise
advanced sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes

items.stem: A person has a far point of 80 cm and a near point of 75 cm. (a) Name the two defects. (b) Find the power of the lens needed to correct distant vision. (c) Find the power needed for reading at 25 cm. (d) What type of spectacles would suit this person? (e) Give one cause of each defect.
items.answer: (a) Myopia and hypermetropia (presbyopia). (b) −1.25 D (concave). (c) +2.67 D (convex). (d) Bifocal lenses – concave upper part, convex lower part. (e) Myopia: elongated eyeball/excess curvature; hypermetropia: short eyeball/long focal length (weak ciliary muscles with age).
items.markingKey: (b) f = −80 cm. (c) 1/f = −1/75 + 1/25 ⇒ f = 37.5 cm. 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Classify these as a result of scattering of light or a result of atmospheric refraction: (1) the wavering of objects seen through hot air above a fire; (2) the flattened appearance of the Sun at sunrise; (3) advanced sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes; (4) the reddish appearance of the Sun at sunset; (5) the blue colour of the clear sky; (6) the black sky seen by astronauts.
items.answer: A result of scattering of light: the black sky seen by astronauts; the blue colour of the clear sky; the reddish appearance of the Sun at sunset. A result of atmospheric refraction: advanced sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes; the flattened appearance of the Sun at sunrise; the wavering of objects seen through hot air above a fire.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A result of scattering of light: the black sky seen by astronauts; the blue colour of the clear sky; the reddish appearance of the Sun at sunset. A result of atmospheric refraction: advanced sunrise and delayed sunset by about 2 minutes; the flattened appearance of the Sun at sunrise; the wavering of objects seen through hot air above a fire.

items.stem: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering the eye?
items.answer: the iris
items.markingKey: (b) The iris — controls the amount of light entering the eye. The others: the ciliary muscles – changes the focal length of the eye lens; the retina – converts light into electrical signals; the cornea – refracts most of the light entering the eye.

items.stem: Isaac Newton showed that white light is made of seven colours by using:
items.answer: a second, inverted prism to recombine the spectrum
items.markingKey: (c) a second, inverted prism to recombine the spectrum.

items.stem: The near point of Ananya's grandfather is 125 cm. What power of lens is needed for him to read a book at 25 cm? Name the defect and the type of lens.
items.answer: Hypermetropia; convex lens of focal length 31.2 cm, power +3.2 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form a virtual image of the book (u = −25 cm) at the near point (v = −125 cm). 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/125 + 1/25 ⇒ f = 31.2 cm; P = 100/f = +3.2 D.

items.stem: The near point of Sneha's grandfather is 50 cm. What power of lens is needed for him to read a book at 25 cm? Name the defect and the type of lens.
items.answer: Hypermetropia; convex lens of focal length 50 cm, power +2 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form a virtual image of the book (u = −25 cm) at the near point (v = −50 cm). 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/50 + 1/25 ⇒ f = 50 cm; P = 100/f = +2 D.

items.stem: Farhan cannot see objects beyond 4 m clearly. Name the defect and find the nature, focal length and power of the lens needed.
items.answer: Myopia; concave lens of focal length −400 cm and power −0.25 D
items.markingKey: The lens must form an image of a distant object at the far point: u = ∞, v = −400 cm ⇒ f = −400 cm = −4 m; P = 1/f = −0.25 D.

items.stem: Which of the two colours, violet or red, is deviated less by a glass prism?
items.answer: red
items.markingKey: (a) Deviation increases from red to violet (VIBGYOR order: violet most, red least).
